tube.e: From Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”), related to tuba (“long trumpet; war-trumpet”), of obscure ultimate origin, but possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-pipe”); see there.
tube.g: Anything that is hollow and cylindrical in shape.

tuck.e: From Middle English tuken, touken (“to torment, to stretch (cloth)”), from Old English tūcian (“to torment, vex”) and Middle Dutch tucken (“to tuck”), both from Proto-Germanic *teuh-, *teug- (“to draw, pull”) (compare also *tukkōną), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull”).
tuck.g: To pull or gather up (an item of fabric).

tuck.e: From Old French estoc (“rapier”), from Italian stocco (“a truncheon, a short sword”).

tumble.e: From Middle English tumblen (“to fall over and over again, tumble”), frequentative of Middle English tumben (“to fall, leap, dance”), from Old English tumbian, from Proto-West Germanic *tumbōn, tūmōn, from Proto-Germanic *tumbōną, tūmōną (“to turn, rotate”).
tumble.g: A fall, especially end over end.

tumor.e: From Middle English tumour, from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“bulge, swell”, verb), from Proto-Italic *tumēō, from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”).
tumor.g: An abnormal growth; differential diagnosis includes abscess, metaplasia, and neoplasia.

tumult.e: From Old French tumulte, from Latin tumultus (“noise, tumult”).
tumult.g: Confused, agitated noise as made by a crowd.

tumultuous.e: From Old French tumultuous (modern French tumultueux), from Latin tumultuōsus (“restless, turbulent”), from tumultus (“disturbance, uproar, violent commotion, tumult; agitation, disturbance, excitement”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns).

tune.e: From Middle English tune, an unexplained variant of tone, from Old French ton, from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “a tone”).

tunic.e: Borrowed from Middle French tunique, from Latin tunica, possibly from Semitic (compare Aramaic (kittuna), Hebrew כותנת (kuttoneth, “coat”), English chiton); or from Etruscan. Existed in Old English as tunece; unknown if that term was lost and then reborrowed later.
tunic.g: A garment worn over the torso, with or without sleeves, and of various lengths reaching from the hips to the ankles.

tunnel.e: From Middle English tonnel, from Old French tonel(e), diminutive of tone (“cask”), a word of uncertain origin and affiliation.

turban.e: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband), also the root of tulip.
turban.g: A man's headdress made by winding a length of cloth round the head.

turbulent.e: From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).
turbulent.g: Violently disturbed or agitated; tempestuous, tumultuous.

turmoil.e: Unknown. First appears c. 1526. Perhaps from Old French tremouille (“the hopper of a mill”).
turmoil.g: A state of great disorder or uncertainty.

turn.e: From Middle English turnen, from Old English turnian, tyrnan (“to turn, rotate, revolve”), from Proto-West Germanic *turnēn (“to turn, lathe”) (also the source of German turnen and its derivatives) and Old French torner (“to turn”), both from Latin tornāre (“to round off, turn in a lathe”), from tornus (“lathe”).
turn.g: To make a non-linear physical movement.

turn.e: Partly from Anglo-Norman *torn, from Latin tornus, from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos), and partly an action noun from the verb turn.
turn.g: A change of direction or orientation.

turning.e: From Middle English turninge, turnynge, turninde, turnand, turnende, from Old English tyrnende, turniende, present participle of Old English tyrnan, turnian (“to turn”). Equivalent to turn + -ing.

turquoise.e: From Middle French turquoise, from Old French (pierre) turquoise (“Turkish (stone)”), from turc + -ois. The stone, mined near Nishapur in the Khorasan region of Persia, was originally brought to Europe through Turkey.
turquoise.g: A sky-blue, greenish-blue, or greenish-gray semi-precious gemstone.

turtle.e: Modification of Middle English tortou, tortu, from Old French tortüe (under the influence of Middle English turtel, turtur (“turtledove”), see Etymology 2 below), from Old Occitan tortuga (compare Spanish tortuga), the same source of tortoise (see there for more).
turtle.g: Any land, aquatic, or semi-aquatic reptile of the order Testudines, characterised by a protective shell enclosing its body. See also tortois

turtle.e: From Middle English turtle, tortle, turtel, turtul, from Old English turtle, turtla (“turtledove”), ultimately from Latin turtur (“turtledove”), of imitative origin.

tusk.e: From Middle English tusk (also tux, tusch), from Old English tūsc, tūx (“canine tooth, tusk, molar”), from Proto-West Germanic *tų̄sk, *tunsk, from Proto-Germanic *tunþskaz (“canine tooth”), extended form of *tanþs (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts (“tooth”).
tusk.g: One of a pair of elongated pointed teeth (either cuspids or incisors) that extend outside the mouth of an animal such as walrus, elephant or

tutor.e: From Middle English tutour, from Old French tuteur (French tuteur), from Latin tūtor (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from tueor (“protect”); see tuition.
tutor.g: One who teaches another (usually called a student, learner, or tutee) in a one-on-one or small-group interaction.

tutor.e: Ellipsis of Demonic tutor, name of an early Magic: The Gathering card with this effect.
tutor.g: A card that allows one to search one's deck for one or more other cards.
